title: Polaronic hybridization of atoms, dimers and trimers in a Bose-Einstein condensate
authors: Carsten Robens, Arthur Christianen, Alexander Y. Chuang, Huan Q. Bui, Yiming Zhang, Richard Schmidt, Martin Zwierlein
abstract: The Bose polaron problem of an impurity immersed in a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) has been predicted to feature strong correlations arising from bound states of multiple bosons with the impurity. While direct experimental evidence has so far remained elusive, here we observe clear signatures of three-body correlations in Bose polarons. We perform radiofrequency spectroscopy on $^{40}$K impurities in a BEC of $^{23}$Na and identify polaronic hybrid states that can be understood as superpositions of the bare atom, a NaK dimer and a Na$_2$K trimer, coupled through coherent particle exchange with the condensate. We show that the main spectroscopic features are captured by a simple three-level model without free parameters. Our work shows how a condensate environment can coherently hybridize bound states of different composition and mass, reminiscent of quark-flavor mixing described by the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix in particle physics.
summary: The research reports on observing three-body correlations in Bose polarons by studying an impurity atom within a BEC. By performing rf spectroscopy and developing a three-level theoretical model, the authors demonstrate that the condensate environment coherently hybridizes molecular bound states (dimer/trimer). This work provides strong evidence for complex many-body interactions in ultracold atomic systems.
main_problem: The study investigates strong correlations, specifically three-body interactions, within Bose polarons formed by an impurity immersed in a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC). The goal is to understand how the BEC environment coherently hybridizes different molecular bound states.
main_result: Clear signatures of three-body correlations are observed spectroscopically, confirming that the ground state eigenstate is a superposition of dimer and trimer components driven by strong BEC coupling. The simple three-level model successfully captures these hybridization effects without requiring free parameters.
method: The work combines theoretical modeling using a three-level Hamiltonian with experimental radiofrequency (rf) spectroscopy on trapped atoms. Variational calculations are used to derive the matrix elements for this effective Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The system involves an impurity atom interacting with a BEC of bosons, leading to polaronic hybridization between bare atomic states, $	ext{NaK}$ dimers, and $	ext{Na}_2	ext{K}$ trimers. The physics is modeled using a three-level Hamiltonian derived from microscopic interactions.
key_observables: Spectroscopic features (energy shifts and broadening), state composition of the ground state eigenstate, and impurity lifetimes ($	ext{1/}\Gamma$).
important_parameters: The system operates in a strong-coupling regime where BEC coupling exceeds intrinsic molecular splittings; key parameters include BEC density and magnetic field tuning near Feshbach resonances.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the assumption that the BEC coupling is strong enough to induce hybridization comparable to or exceeding intrinsic molecular splittings. Theoretical models use approximations like the Born approximation for interboson repulsion.
figures_summary: Figures show spatially resolved spectra confirming signal dependence on density, energy eigenvalue plots illustrating state superposition vs. density, and lifetime measurements distinguishing between attractive and repulsive polaron branches.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical problem (three-body correlations in polarons) to developing a simple three-level model Hamiltonian. It details experimental spectroscopy using rf pulses and compares theoretical predictions of hybridization energies and state weights against measured spectral features across varying BEC densities.
why_interesting: This work provides an excellent example of how complex many-body physics (three-body correlations) can be mapped onto a simple, experimentally verifiable effective Hamiltonian (three-level model), drawing parallels to fundamental concepts in particle physics like CKM mixing.

(b) Illustration of the wave function: a superposition of a free K-atom, a dimer, and a trimer. (c) The effective Hamiltonian in the basis of these three states. (d) The three eigenvalues of this Hamiltonian as a function of the BEC density n0. The widths and opacities of the colored sub-lines represent the co- efficients |c1|2 (blue), |c2|2 (green) and |c3|2 (red) for each of the eigenstates. The horizontal dashed lines indicate the en- ergies of the three bare basis states.

FIG. 2. Radiofrequency spectra of 40K impurities strongly depend on their position in the 23Na BEC. (a) Density profile of the BEC, where the grayscale indicates the optical density (OD). (b) Spatially resolved spectra at B = 102.5G of initial state |↓⟩depletion when driving at given detuning from the |↓⟩-|↑⟩bare hyperfine transition. The solid lines indicate the theory predictions from the three-level model, whereas the dashed line shows the theory result without three-body cor- relations.

FIG. 4. Lifetimes of the states created by rf injection. These lifetimes are inferred from the ratio of population de- pleted from |↓⟩to population observed in |↑⟩(upper panels and Fig. 3). For data taken at B ≤105 G, we resolve the attractive and repulsive branches of the spectrum, whereas for larger magnetic fields the two features merge (see upper panels). The lifetime of the attractive polaron states (green circles) decreases at deeper binding energy, whereas the life- time of the repulsive polaron branch (red squares) increases. Blue diamonds: lifetime of the merged feature above 105 G. At sufficiently deep binding energies, we do not observe any population in |↓⟩.

Note the double peak structure corresponding to the dimer and trimer feature for the lowest density spectrum, taken with a thermal, uncondensed bosonic cloud.
